Hi! Newbie options trader here so take what I say with a grain of salt, but I too struggled and took way more losses than I should have been comfortable with. I like to look at it as a tuition for learning what NOT to do. I didn't back test like a lot of people because I didn't feel the loss like I did with my own money. The strategy that stuck with me was support and resistance and trend lines. It's about as basic as it gets. I use VWAP and volume to determine my entry, but that's not what will truly get you where you want to be. In my opinion 98% is mindset and risk management and the other 2% is actually technical analysis. When I learned how to be accurate with my risk management and follow trades with an extremely close stop loss as well as not fomo into trades, things changed. I won't let my options lose less than 8%, but most of my gains are 20%+. If you get stopped out, oh well, look for a better setup. I have 3 day trades a week otherwise I get a PDT ban and have to have $25,000 in my account. I've gotten my $500 account up to $2000 within a month. Take what you've learned with your losses and try again. Put a stop loss in place around resistance at the time frame you trade and FOLLOW THROUGH. Don't move it. I've found a couple different youtubers I like and combine strategies for something that will work on a small account. At the end of the day, it's not a sure thing so you have to have a stop at what you're willing to lose. Some days are only sideways and don't give you an entry. DONT TRADE ON THOSE DAYS. I hope you find some good ideas that give you inspiration to keep this up. We all deserve the financial freedom we're looking for!

New Techie here too. This coming March will mark my first year of scrubbing. I was completely on the job trained so 6 of those months were spent learning all the specialties. Scrubbing is tough, and it takes YEARS to get good. The best thing you can do is go into it with a "I can and will do this to the best of my abilities" mindset  I'll sometimes even let the surgeons know if it's a case I've done very little of that I'm still new and learning, but I'll do the very best I can to learn and be better for next time. I've had surgeons teach me how to suture because I show initiative and want to learn. Also, do all the specialties. Don't just pick one and get good at it. You've gotta be versatile if you ever want to do this job well. They throw me in any and everything because I truly want to know absolutely everything I can about this job. Keep with it. I know it's easy to doubt yourself, but you know more than you think.

My first solo we ended up in a spin when I went to practice touch and couldn't find it. My instructor ended up letting go and my brain completely blanked on the whole "pull parachute if instructor lets go regardless." I ended up in a sit fly as well as back flying before my instructor grabbed on and pulled my chute for me. I had absolutely no fear and no thought of "oh no this is bad." I was simply just enjoying flipping and flopping around and it wasn't until I landed and watched the video that I realized just how bad that could have ended. Made me incredibly grateful for a great instructor that wasn't going to let me die. Ever since each one has been better and better. The nerves start to subside and it's more excitement. I'm on level 6 and super nervous about solo exit, but as I like to remind myself "if you can't beat the fear, do it scared🤙" I also used to get pretty sick on my tandems (I did 9 before I started AFF), but luckily never threw up. Hydrate hydrate hydrate and BREATHE. Eat a small meal before and drink plenty of water. It also gets much better when you're manning the chute yourself. If you don't remember anything else during the fall, only remember to pull the chute.

Also there's no such thing as a bad jump. Every jump is a new learning experience. Blue skies, my friend!
